children: MARKET WRAPS
STOCKS: Stocks fell as Treasury yields hit multiyear highs due to escalation in the Iran war.
TREASURYS: Treasury yields rose and yields on the two-year and 10-year notes closed at 2026 highs due to anticipation of further energy inflation.
FOREX: The U.S. dollar ticked down against rivals as traders hedged their bets ahead of inflation data later in the week.
COMMODITIES: Oil futures rose after Houthi rebels reportedly struck a Saudi Aramco refinery.
HEADLINES
Iran Launched Undisclosed Second Wave of Attacks on U.S. Navy Ships
Iran launched an attack against U.S. Navy ships on Monday that the
U.S. military has yet to acknowledge, according to U.S. officials, after
firing ballistic missiles at an aircraft carrier and a guided-missile
destroyer over the weekend.
No American ships were struck in the attacks, but Iran's recent
attempts to hit American naval assets are raising alarm that its military
is using more sophisticated weapons and could be getting assistance from
China or Russia, according to the officials.
The attacks highlight Iran's willingness to go on the offensive as the
U.S. blockade of Iranian ports weighs on the country's economy. They also
risk escalating the conflict, since the U.S. has promised to take action
against such attacks.
Canada's Carney Vows to Backstop Economy as U.S. Trade Row Escalates
OTTAWA-Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said his government will
"do whatever it takes" to backstop regions and industrial sectors
targeted by U.S. tariffs as the trade conflict between the neighboring
and closely-integrated economies enters a precarious stage.
In an address posted on YouTube, Carney said retaliatory tariffs on
about $20 billion in U.S. goods that kicked in on Tuesday were necessary
to protect domestic sectors and workers. "I don't believe in escalating
the conflict," said Carney. "The harsh reality is that the American
tariffs will hurt some Canadians or others, and that was by design."
As a result, "we will do whatever it takes for as long as it takes to
bridge those people" in affected sectors "to a better future," he said.
Carney added that his Liberal government would in the meantime pursue
policies that reduce dependence on trade with the U.S. to power growth,
although warning this would present economic turbulence.
Ford's Use of Chinese Tech Called 'Unacceptable' by Transportation
Secretary
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy sharply criticized Ford Motor's
business with Chinese automotive firms, saying the company's "reliance on
technologies of foreign adversaries" isn't sustainable for America.
"While DOT recognizes the intense competitive pressures of the global
market, the company's recent strategic decisions paint a troubling
picture of a foundational American brand actively intertwining its future
with Chinese state-backed enterprises," Duffy said in a letter to Ford
Chief Executive Jim Farley made public Tuesday.
Duffy also called the manufacturing of Lincoln vehicles in China for
the U.S. market "unacceptable." While Ford has said it would re-shore
production of those vehicles starting in 2030, Duffy said the years in
between represent a "multi-year window of reliance on Chinese
manufacturing while depriving skilled American workers of vital
manufacturing jobs."
What to Know About Anthropic's Planned IPO
Wall Street's marquee event this fall is expected to be Anthropic's
initial public offering. It could raise up to $100 billion and value the
artificial-intelligence giant at around $2 trillion, The Wall Street
Journal has reported. Those figures would top records set by SpaceX's
debut in June.
Investors are still waiting for a peek at the company's inner
financial workings, and the company still has key decisions to make.
Anthropic confidentially filed its IPO paperwork with the Securities
and Exchange Commission in June. The next step is making that paperwork
public ahead of an investor roadshow and the actual listing.
Amazon Sued for Allegedly Discriminating Against Pregnant Employees
A group of former Amazon.com warehouse employees is suing the company,
alleging they were illegally punished and eventually terminated for
seeking accommodations related to their pregnancies.
The class-action, led by four ex-warehouse workers, alleges that
Amazon deducted their bank of unpaid time off or flagged them for "time
off-task" for medically necessary breaks or absences.
One plaintiff was flagged for excessive time off-task for pumping in
the company's lactation room, the lawsuit said.
GE Aerospace to Buy Consolidated Precision Products for $11.75 Billion
GE Aerospace agreed to buy metal-castings provider Consolidated
Precision Products for $11.75 billion, placing a large bet on the
advanced materials needed to keep its advanced engines cool.
The engine maker said its purchase from private investment firms
Warburg Pincus and Berkshire Partners will help the Evendale, Ohio,
company meet surging demand for its engines. About 60% of the CPP's
revenue came from commercial aerospace customers, with the remainder from
defense, power and other markets.
GE Aerospace said it plans to fund the acquisition, slated to close in
the second half of 2027, with $7 billion in cash on hand and the
remainder in new debt, adding that the deal doesn't change its
capital-allocation plans.
Verizon, Corning Reach Multi-Billion Dollar Agreement for Broadband
Expansion
Verizon and Corning reached a multibillion-dollar agreement to deploy
more than 80 million miles of high-density optical fiber across the
nation over the coming five years.
The companies on Tuesday said the deal will help meet surging demand
for consumer broadband and converged services, accelerating Verizon's
push to bring internet access to more homes and businesses across the
nation.
The deal will also help build out the national long-haul backbone
required by AI hyperscalers, supporting emerging artificial intelligence
needs, the companies added.
Boston Scientific Won't Meet Guidance Due to Cyberattack
Boston Scientific said it likely won't meet its financial guidance due
to the cyberattack that has disrupted its operations, sending shares of
the medical-technology company down sharply in premarket trading.
Boston Scientific on Tuesday said it continues to make progress in
restoring many of its systems that were affected by the hack, including
substantial restoration of its distribution network, but that it expects
to miss its sales and adjusted per-share earnings guidance for the
third-quarter and full year.
Shares of the Marlborough, Mass., company were recently down 4% to
$45.90 in early trading.
U.S. Gets Minority Stakes in Some Quantum Computing Companies in $300
Million CHIPS Act Funding Deal
The U.S. government is taking minority equity stakes in D-Wave
Quantum, Rigetti Computing, and Quantinuum with a combined $300 million
CHIPS Act deal that funds the three companies to scale quantum-computing
research.
The companies will each receive $100 million from the U.S. Department
of Commerce, structured as a research-and-development grant under the
CHIPS Act, the companies said Tuesday. As part of the grants, the
Commerce Department will take a minority stake in each of the three
companies as it looks to support the development of domestic
semiconductor and advanced-hardware supply chains.
Quantinuum shares rose 5.5% to $52.44, while D-Wave shares climbed
9.1% to $18.08. Rigetti's stock advanced 6.4% to $16.17.
U.S. Employment Trends Index Rose in August, Conference Board Says
A reading of the U.S. labor market from The Conference Board moved up
in August, with signs that underemployment is easing and perceptions of
job availability are improving, a gauge of employment showed.
The Employment Trends Index, or ETI, rose to 108.53, from an upwardly revised 107.76 in July.
The move continues a rebound that started last month after declines in
May and June and brings the index up 2% higher than where it was a year
ago, said Conrad Qi, an economic data scientist associate at The
Conference Board.
TALKING POINT Bank Preferred Stocks Are Sending a Warning About Interest Rates

Preferred shares issued by major U.S. banks such as Bank of America Corp. and Wells Fargo & Co. differ sharply from their common stock. They typically carry a fixed dividend that must be paid before any common dividend, rank senior in the capital structure during liquidation, and generally confer no voting rights.

Because most bank preferreds are perpetual and trade like long-duration bonds, their market prices are highly sensitive to interest-rate expectations rather than the banks' earnings growth. Consequently, the recent behavior of these securities provides an important indication of the rate outlook.

The lack of a meaningful rally in bank preferreds suggests investors are not yet pricing in a sustained decline in interest rates. In other words, the preferred market continues to lean toward a "higher-for-longer" rate regime, with expectations for meaningful cuts in the near term remaining subdued.
Here's a look at the weakness in Bank of America and Wells Fargo preferreds, along with the stubbornly high 10-year Treasury yield, now near 4.8%.

A look at Bank of America Series QQ this year shows that the softness began with the bearish death cross in March. Notice the gap down on May 1, followed by a bullish inverse head-and-shoulders formation that took shape through May and June. The brief breakout above the pattern and the 50-day simple moving average failed in late June, leading to a bear flag formation.

A bullish morning star completed on August 18, indicating selling pressure was abating. However, Friday's break below the $16 pivot shifts the setup back to the bearish side. The shares could move lower toward $14.75 in the near term, representing an 8% decline from current prices.
Doug Busch
